This user guide provides a brief explanation of the main data types and functionality of Larecs﻿🌲. For new users it is advisable to go through it in the order of the side menu.
For a deeper dive into ECS and the architecture by Larecs🌲, have a look at the ECS FAQ by Sander Mertens, the author of the Flecs ECS and the architecture section of the Arche ECS by Martin Lange, which served as the main inspiration for Larecs🌲.

Adding and removing individual entities is done via the add_entity and remove_entity methods of World.storage. Revisiting our earlier example of a world with Position and Velocity, this reads as follows:
The examples in this chapter mutate a World directly to demonstrate its storage API. This is useful for setup and isolated changes. In application logic, these operations should generally be performed by a system through its SystemContext.
from larecs import World, Filter, SystemContext, KernelContext @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 def place_batch(rows: KernelContext[Filter().include[Position]()]): """Places each execution-local row one unit farther along the x axis.""" for row in rows: row.get[Position]().x = Float64(row.idx) def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add an entity and get its representation var entity = world.storage.add_entity() # Remove the entity world.storage.remove_entity(entity) Components can be added to the entities directly upon creation. For example, to create an entity with a position at (0, 0) and a velocity of (1, 0), we can do the following:
entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) place_batch uses row.idx, which restarts at zero for each selected host range; it does not assign globally unique indices.
data.batch-addition#Batch addition:
Systems create batches through add_entities. The result is a movable, noncopyable EntitySelection containing exactly the new rows and owning the world’s structural-change lock:
var context = SystemContext(world) var created = context.add_entities( Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0), count=10 ) created.run[place_batch]() created^.release() Use a with block to release the lock automatically, including when an error or early return exits the block:
with context.add_entities(Position(0, 0), count=10) as selected: selected.add(Velocity(1, 0)) selected.run[place_batch]() selected.run[place_batch]() # The structural lock is released here. For an existing selection, write with selection^ as selected: to transfer ownership into the manager. The bound selection cannot escape the block’s manager. The manager retains the lock until exit, even if the bound selection is consumed or explicitly released inside the block.
Note
A selection can run kernels repeatedly. Component-changing methods update its membership in place and retain the same lock; they return nothing. Call selection^.release() when finished, or let it be destroyed. While it lives, unrelated creation, deletion, and archetype changes are rejected. An empty selection is still locked and follows the same rule.
The lower-level HostStorage.add_entities remains available for setup code, and returns iteration.LockedEntityRange (also named by the HostStorage.Iterator type alias). It borrows storage and its lock manager, records exact bounded batch rows, and supports len, Bool, iteration, and mutable unsafe_get access. Copies share membership metadata but retain independent cursor positions and structural locks; moves transfer the existing lock. Exhaustion, including an empty result, retains the lock until destruction. Use SystemContext.add_entities and a selection kernel for system logic; a storage range has no .run, .add, .remove, or .release method.
The beta concrete return type LockedWorldEntityIterator was renamed to LockedEntityRange; explicit HostStorage.Iterator specializations use has_ranges=True instead of has_start_indices=True. Inferred storage loops need no change. See decision 0022.
data.batch-removal#Batch removal:
If we want to remove multiple entities at once, we need to characterize which entities we mean. To that end, we use queries, which characterize entities by their components. For example, removing all entities that have the component Position can be done with remove_entities as follows:
# Remove all entities that have a Position component world.storage.remove_entities[Filter().include[Position]()]() More on queries can be found in the chapter Queries and iteration.
Tip
Prefer the batch operations when you add or remove many entities. add_entities looks up the target archetype once and grows its columns once for the whole batch, while add_entity repeats both steps per entity. remove_entities clears each matching archetype as a whole instead of removing its rows one at a time. How much this saves depends on the batch size and on the component types.

The focused entity_selection_benchmark.mojo workload compares ordinary full-world host execution with contiguous and disjoint 64-row selections in a 100,000-row world, a selected add/remove chain, and selected device execution when an accelerator is available. On the Apple Metal development host used for the 1.0.0b2 work, one bounded run measured approximately 0.0253 ms for the 100k-row host path, 0.0000664 ms for the contiguous selection, 0.000556 ms for 64 disjoint single-row ranges, 0.00727 ms for the add/remove chain, and 0.379 ms for the device selection. These are development measurements, not a cross-version historical baseline; use the benchmark on target hardware for regression decisions.
The manual host thread dispatch experiment compares complete sequential kernel calls with dynamically claimed whole-store and contiguous chunk jobs at 1/2/4 worker tasks, including small and large increment/compute workloads and single-store cases. Its driver, timing boundaries, reproduction commands, and Linux measurements are recorded there. It is a restricted feasibility benchmark; the current experimental engine adds eligibility and lifecycle checks absent from that prototype. Both drivers remain outside the normal PR performance gate.
data.benchmark-methodology#Benchmark methodol:
Build a focused manual driver once with pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/<benchmark_filename>.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-benchmark, then run /tmp/larecs-benchmark repeatedly. Run the complete manual suite with pixi run mojo run -I src benchmark/run_benchmarks.mojo.
When changing storage, queries, classification, row movement, or execution costs, add or update representative benchmarks using these criteria:
Keep the combined PR performance checks near one minute per runner, including compilation, warmup, and sampling. Measure cold compilation and execution separately on Linux and macOS before expanding the suite. Keep large worlds, GPU cases, and the complete benchmark registry in focused manual drivers. Use deterministic inputs, bounded calibration or fixed iteration counts, and a compact scenario matrix. Spatial cases should cover uniform, dense, sparse, and moving entities with different maintenance cadences. Compare identical entities and semantic work, with an unchanged-layout control. Measure isolated operations and complete frames when useful. Include input updates, classification, sorting, movement, location repair, and transfers whenever they belong to the claimed workload. State excluded setup and maintenance costs; validate results, locations, and payload preservation outside the timer, and consume results to prevent dead-code elimination. Build each timing binary once, then run it repeatedly. Compare the same current driver against baseline and current libraries on the same runner with matching compiler versions and optimization settings. Use optimized builds without debug info, sanitizers, or tracing. Run builds and measurements sequentially, with no competing benchmark jobs, and report compilation separately. Warm both binaries, alternate baseline/current order, and use repeated paired samples. Keep machine-specific timing baselines out of the repository. See PR performance checks and spatial checks for baseline selection, thresholds, confirmation, and support for revisions predating the spatial API. Keep the small regression checks in pixi run tests test on Linux and macOS; focused test-file runs omit performance checks. Investigate sustained failures and document evidence before changing thresholds; use dedicated measurements for smaller regressions. Keep scenario matrices and expected-case manifests synchronized. Invalid or incomplete reports, build failures, and correctness failures must fail checks. Update this guide when changing cases, timing boundaries, sampling, or baseline selection. Record hardware, compiler, method, and limitations with performance claims; track unmeasured benefits and remaining work in the roadmap.
data.deferred-dirty-classification#Deferred d:
Build pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/dirty_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-dirty-spatial, then run that binary with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. It constructs identical scrambled 2,048/32,768-entity worlds with 72 component bytes per row plus entity IDs, establishes initial spatial order, warms both paths, and alternates five paired samples of sixteen frames (1,024 frames for clean boundaries to resolve their small cost). The 24 scenarios cover uniform (16 entities/cell), dense (256/cell), and sparse (16/cell with key gaps of 128) distributions, with 0, 1, 1/64, or all identities updated. Each updated identity receives two reference writes per frame; classification observes final values. On alternating frames those writes cancel. Other frames advance cells by one. Both paths perform identical updates and semantic work.
The deferred path uses automatic tracking. Its control requests a full rebuild after those same writes. Timings include updates, marking, key scratch allocation, classification, sorting, typed movement of all columns, and location repair. Construction, registration, initial maintenance, and correctness checks are excluded. Every sample validates complete key order, each identity/location, the expected final input for every identity, and all eight payload lanes outside timing through read-only queries. Output records rows, distribution, dirty count, pair number, and deferred/full frame ns. This compares current deferred maintenance with current explicit full rebuilds; it does not measure a historical implementation or total application speedup.
Clean calls do no row work. Dirty calls still copy O(entity-ID capacity) keys and inspect affected archetypes, so sparse classification is not O(D) complete maintenance. Full rebuilds currently reset sparse membership and caches. Dense updates may favor contiguous full classification; structural-heavy workloads use full rebuilds. Retained keys/membership cost at least nine bytes per allocated ID plus queue capacity (full ID/generation identities and allocator slack). Scratch and movement metadata add temporary memory. These are layout costs, not measured application memory usage.
A local run on Apple M4, arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567) with implementation 76868ef (based on 0241e91) built the optimized driver in 4.74 seconds. Five warmed pairs gave these median complete-frame times for 32,768 entities:
Distribution Dirty identities Deferred Explicit full rebuild Deferred/full Uniform 1 0.685 ms 1.076 ms 0.637 Uniform 512 0.749 ms 1.133 ms 0.661 Dense 512 0.811 ms 1.194 ms 0.679 Sparse 1 0.097 ms 0.490 ms 0.198 Sparse 512 0.112 ms 0.497 ms 0.226 Uniform 32,768 0.850 ms 0.858 ms 0.991 Across both sizes and all distributions, nonzero sparse-update scenarios took 19.5–67.9% of the full-rebuild frame time. Clean boundaries measured approximately 3–4 ns (close to timer resolution), versus 0.031/0.490 ms full rebuilds at the two sizes. Fully dirty frames took 99.1–104.6% of the explicit control. An earlier version that resolved every dirty identity separately took 131–141% for fully dirty frames; the accepted all-ID-dirty fallback avoids that column/location setup cost. Neither path can avoid moving clean rows when regrouping demands it.
The separate same-driver PR gate against 0241e91 passed all 12 core and 32 spatial cases in 41.1 seconds including four sequential compilations and five paired samples. It found no confirmed regression under the existing 30%/500 ns rule. It still measured approximately 15–19% overhead for reversing maintenance, 10–14% for maintained mobile frames, and 3–8% for ordinary stable-ID access. Those costs remain visible tradeoffs, not claims of zero regression. Linux evidence comes from the PR checks; actual GPU execution is validated separately and is not included in these CPU performance numbers.
data.partitioned-storage-comparison#Partition:
Build the optimized standalone driver once: pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/partitioned_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-partition-benchmark. Run that binary without concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Partitioning is explicitly selected at registration; the control is the same current library’s deferred row reordering, not forced full classification or a historical library with different invalidation costs. The existing core/spatial PR gate separately measures changes to the default paths against the exact base.
The driver constructs identical deterministic scrambled 2,048/32,768-row worlds with two component-defined archetypes, 64-byte SIMD payloads, an integer input, and an additional eight-byte column on half the rows. It compares one growable store per logical cluster with row reordering for uniform (16 identities per cell), dense (1,024 per cell), and singleton sparse (one identity per cell, key spacing 128) distributions. Each configuration warms both layouts with one sixteen-frame batch, then alternates their order for five paired sixteen-frame samples.
The 48 scenarios cover maintenance with 1, 1/64, or all identities updated; ordinary read-only query scans and host execution with unchanged layouts; and complete cell frames with the same updates, maintenance every frame (or every fourth frame for 1/64 updates), all-lane per-cell aggregation, and cyclic adjacent-cell aggregate products. Both layouts use identical entities, input updates, and semantic work. The scan controls still call the clean boundary. All measured update frames include marking, pending key allocation/copy, classification, directory construction or sorting, column growth/movement, source swap-removal, location repair, and allocation reclamation as applicable. Cell frames also include query setup, cell scratch allocation, aggregation, and neighbor arithmetic. Construction, initial placement, policy/device setup, and validation are excluded. There are no device transfers in these CPU timings.
Every sample checks all identities once, final inputs, all payload lanes, entity locations, default key order or homogeneous cluster stores, and equal complete spatial checksums outside timing. Query/host scan reductions are also checked against their complete expected sums. Results are consumed inside the timer. This is a synthetic spatial workload, not a game/simulation speedup, collision detection, or a persistent neighbor index.
MEMORY records report initial maintained capacity-derived owned bytes; MEMORY_AFTER_MOVEMENT reports retained buffers after 96 fully moving frames: physical-directory slots, component/ID buffers, entity locations, key/dirty caches, queued identities, and recycled-slot capacity. Counted allocations are physical-directory plus row-column/ID allocations. Graph/pool allocations, allocator overhead, device state, classifier configuration, and all temporary maintenance/query/cell scratch are excluded; these records are not RSS or peak memory measurements. The components are trivial and have no hidden payload heap. Columns in a store share capacity, but each column and the IDs allocate separately. PAIR records give rows, distribution, mode, update count, cadence, pair index, reordering ns/frame, and partition ns/frame.
Growable-store comparison on Linux The same current driver was built against committed base df0e6c5638beaab2bf3784a2b4784044a7c2707e (256-row-capped blocks) and the growable-store implementation from decision 0014. This local run used AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 7.2.5-3-omarchy x86_64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), normal optimized builds without tracing, sanitizers, or debug information. Cold builds ran sequentially and took 11.13 s / 11.11 s (base/current). No other builds or benchmark jobs ran during timing; background desktop services remained active. Five pairs of fresh binary invocations alternated base/current order. Each invocation used the warmup, five paired sixteen-frame samples per case, timing boundaries, and complete validation described above. Values below are medians of the five per-invocation medians, in milliseconds. All 48 cases validated in all ten invocations. Median complete driver execution including validation was 13.10 s / 11.33 s (base/current).
Driver SHA-256: 37795c49baa95f1b911d43327d413097b85a5f60f92f3137accf7abfa9a90ad9.
Distribution Timed work, 32,768 rows Capped blocks Growable stores Growable / capped Uniform Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.416 0.256 0.61 Dense Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.111 0.072 0.65 Dense Complete frame, all moving 6.032 4.295 0.71 Singleton sparse Complete frame, all moving 20.400 17.231 0.84 Dense Ordinary query scan, clean 0.430 0.427 0.99 Dense Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.030 0.031 1.03 Uniform Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.068 0.070 1.03 Singleton sparse Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.337 0.344 1.02 Dense initial placement used 64 stores and 225 counted allocations, versus 128 blocks and 449 allocations in the base. Initial counted owned bytes fell from 4,448,265 to 4,403,209. After 96 fully moving frames, growable dense stores retained 7,847,945 bytes and 64,512 row slots, versus 5,062,665 bytes and 32,768 slots for capped blocks. Destination stores can grow while their old rows are still awaiting transfer, and nonempty stores retain that spare capacity. Fewer stores therefore do not guarantee less retained memory. Full scans changed by -0.8% to +4.3% across these distributions; small timing differences on this desktop runner do not establish a scan improvement. Maintenance and fully moving frame results favor growable stores here, but singleton clusters still have separate allocations and substantial traversal overhead. This is CPU-only synthetic evidence; macOS, GPU, application, peak memory, and additional component-width comparisons remain on the roadmap. Local raw reports are retained under output/performance/growable_clusters/.
Historical bounded-block comparison on macOS The measurements below are historical evidence for decision 0013’s 256-row-capped blocks, not timings for the current growable-store layout. Dense clusters now use fewer stores; sparse clusters still require separate allocations. Rerun the driver before making performance claims about the new layout.

Component capacity alone therefore understates partition overhead: physical-store metadata and many separate allocations matter, especially for singleton clusters. At 2,048 rows counted bytes were 273,801 for reordering versus 452,617 uniform, 278,025 dense, and 1,714,185 singleton partition storage. After 96 fully moving frames, counted retained bytes were 4,883,849 for reordering versus 10,116,809 uniform, 5,062,665 dense, and 51,019,785 singleton partitions at 32,768 rows. Small dense/uniform updates took less elapsed maintenance time with partitions, while directory rebuilding and per-block scans dominated singleton cases. The benchmark measures total elapsed costs, not byte-movement counters. Fully moving workloads were slower despite local transfer. Keep partitions opt-in, and retain the reordering default. The measured bounded-block implementation copied identity-capacity keys, inspected blocks, and could move unchanged rows during same-cluster compaction. The current layout retains key copying and directory scans but removes cross-block compaction; destination growth can still relocate existing columns. Cluster selection scans metadata. Application workloads, other component widths, structural-heavy frames, Linux comparative timings, process/peak memory, and device timings remain on the roadmap. GPU functional integration ran on the actual local accelerator; it is separate evidence from these CPU performance measurements.
The separate default-path PR gate against 6037850 passed all twelve core and 32 spatial cases in 49.2 seconds, including four sequential builds and five paired samples. It required no regression confirmation. Ordinary 2,048-row query/host execution changes were +0.1%/-0.6%, stable-ID access was +3.9%, and selected mutation was +0.9% in that run. These small shared-machine differences are not a zero-overhead guarantee; the existing 30%/500 ns rule is unchanged. Hosted Linux/macOS evidence is retained by the PR checks.
data.pr-to-pr-performance-checks#PR-to-PR per:
pixi run performance-check --base <revision> compares the current library with another Git revision on the same machine. Without --base, local runs compare the working tree against committed HEAD; GitHub PR runs use the exact PR base SHA, and main-branch push runs use the previous push commit. The tested current revision is the checkout SHA (normally the PR merge commit in CI). The complete pixi run tests test command runs the gate on Linux and macOS following correctness tests. Focused test-file runs omit it.
The coordinator builds the same current driver against both source trees with the installed Mojo compiler, using optimized builds without tracing, debug information, or sanitizers. It warms both binaries, then runs five pairs, alternating baseline/current order. A case becomes a candidate only if four pairs and the paired medians show over 30% slowdown and over 500 ns extra operation/frame time. Candidates are checked in a fresh five-pair round; only candidates recurring in both rounds fail. Invalid/incomplete reports, incorrect results, compilation failures, unavailable baselines, and timeouts fail rather than silently skipping coverage.
The two focused drivers avoid the expensive complete benchmark registry:
Core case Sizes Timed work Excluded setup and validation access 512/2,048 matching rows Stable-ID component reads and integer checksum World construction; exact per-entity payload checks query 512/2,048 matching rows Fresh filtered iterator, row visits, and checksum Construction of two matching archetypes and equally many excluded tag-only rows; payload checks execute 512/2,048 rows Ordinary host dispatch and integer increments Construction; check every row’s accumulated increments selected_execute 64 selected rows amid 512/2,048 background rows Host dispatch over a reusable contiguous selection Construction and selection creation/release; selected and untouched-row checks selected_mutation Same selection/background sizes Add/remove a tag, including partial-archetype movement and location repair Construction; final membership, absence of tags, payload, and background-location checks batch_cycle 512/2,048 rows Batch creation, payload initialization, removal, and recycling World construction and first validation/warmup cycle; recycled payload, membership, and surviving control-row checks Core calibration doubles from 8 to at most 8,192 operations, stopping at 5 ms per case. Fast cases can reach the cap first. Each duration is per complete operation, not per entity. Read cases consume the checksum inside the timer; execution writes are checked after timing, with observable lengths consumed inside the timer. Spatial boundaries and its unchanged matrix are below.
Run one driver with pixi run core-benchmarks or pixi run spatial-benchmarks. Select a gate with pixi run performance-check --suite core --base <revision> or --suite spatial; repeat --suite to select multiple drivers. The original pixi run spatial-performance-check remains a spatial-only compatibility command.
Reports default to the ignored output/performance/ directory; use --output to choose another directory. report.json includes the schema version, requested/resolved/effective baselines, current checkout SHA and dirty state, driver SHA-256 hashes, compiler, OS/CPU, thresholds, compilation and sampling costs, all paired measurements, and both confirmation rounds when needed. summary.md gives median times, paired changes, candidates, and confirmed failures. Candidates whose confirmation did not finish are labeled unconfirmed; only a completed confirmation can label a candidate transient. Process logs retain build, warmup, execution, and error diagnostics. GitHub adds the Markdown to the job summary and uploads the reports/logs as performance-<runner>-<attempt> artifacts for 30 days, including failed checks. This uses read-only PR permissions and works without publishing PR comments. Require the existing build/test checks in branch protection to enforce the gate.
The initial unchanged-library comparison against 688fb67 on Apple M4, macOS 27 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), took 55.3 seconds: core builds 9.3/9.6 seconds and sampling 2.6 seconds; spatial builds 5.8/5.4 seconds and sampling 22.2 seconds. Builds and samples ran sequentially; no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. These are driver compilation costs in an already installed environment, not dependency installation time.
The first hosted run compared the same unchanged library against 688fb67, using PR merge checkout ba8b180, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the same current driver on each side, fresh output binaries, sequential compilation/sampling, and five alternating pairs. Both suites passed without confirmation, and both artifact uploads succeeded:
Runner CPU / OS All driver builds All sampling Total gate macos-latest Apple M2 Pro (Virtual), macOS 26.6.2 arm64 43.1 s 22.1 s 66.1 s ubuntu-latest AMD EPYC 7763, Linux 6.17 x86_64 / glibc 2.39 50.2 s 24.6 s 75.3 s These are one-run runtime measurements, not speed comparisons between platforms or evidence that the runner’s load is stable. Full correctness tests, examples, package checks, and environment installation are excluded from these gate costs. The combined check stays near a minute; further coverage requires new budget measurements on both platforms. Confirmation adds sampling cost for affected suites; command deadlines bound failures rather than promising a one-minute runtime for all error/confirmation paths.
There are no checked-in machine-specific golden timings. Driver changes affect both sides; compare historical evidence only when hashes and environments are compatible. Compiler upgrades do not measure compiler-to-compiler changes. These broad thresholds target substantial regressions on shared runners; smaller or cumulative regressions, larger worlds, heap-backed payloads, disjoint selections, and device costs need focused measurements or future coverage. See decision 0011 and the roadmap.
data.resource-execution#Resource execution:
resource_execution_benchmark.mojo uses the current execution API. Compare the same workload against the base library, adapting only backend call spelling when the base predates ExecutionBackend. It measures complete calls over 512 Int32 rows with either no resources or one legacy scalar resource. resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo measures current read-only adapters over the same rows and 4,096 initial Int32 samples. Only the first sample is read; the entire source is uploaded. Each timed adapter call edits that sample, and growth cases append one sample per call. Host calls use 10,000 iterations; GPU calls use 100. One warmup invocation precedes each timer. Construction and final checks are excluded; validation, leases, component transfers, resource uploads/downloads, allocation growth, and synchronization are included when applicable. Exact outputs, row counts, source values, and final sample lengths are checked outside timing.
Copy the current driver for the baseline build:
cp benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo /tmp/resource_base.mojo If the base accepts on_device: Bool rather than backend: ExecutionBackend, adapt only that copy before compiling it:
python - <<'PYCODE' from pathlib import Path import re path = Path("/tmp/resource_base.mojo") source = path.read_text().replace(" ExecutionBackend,\n", "") source, count = re.subn( r"backend=\(\s*ExecutionBackend\.DEVICE if device else ExecutionBackend\.HOST\s*\)", "on_device=device", source, ) assert count == 4, "Review the driver before adapting a changed call matrix" assert "ExecutionBackend" not in source.split('from std.time', 1)[1] path.write_text(source) PYCODE This maps the same compile-time device boolean to the older keyword; kernels, row counts, iterations, warmup, validation, and timing boundaries stay identical. Do not substitute a historical driver with different workloads. Device comparisons require a working accelerator on both sides; an older host fallback is not a device measurement. For a base using on_gpu, use that keyword instead.
Build optimized binaries once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing:
pixi run mojo build -I /path/to/base/src /tmp/resource_base.mojo -o /tmp/resource-base pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-current pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-adapters On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), compare base 6a3841b against this implementation with the same driver. Warm each binary, then run five paired samples, alternating base/current order, with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Median per-call means were:
Complete invocation Base Current Host, no resource 294.2 ns 299.6 ns Host, legacy scalar resource 299.8 ns 350.7 ns GPU, no resource 250.50 µs 251.52 µs GPU, legacy scalar resource 243.51 µs 268.59 µs Host, edited adapter — 449.1 ns Host, edited adapter plus growth — 451.4 ns GPU, edited adapter — 323.76 µs GPU, edited adapter plus growth — 303.54 µs The scalar GPU case costs about 10.3% more with staged publication and lifetime protection. These measurements establish the cost of this synthetic workload, not an application speedup or Tree-D shading result. Short GPU batches are noisy; the growth-case ordering does not establish a growth benefit. Source/sample allocation and scientific preprocessing during initial construction are excluded; incremental host append and device allocation growth are included in growth cases. Existing allocation capacity is reused in nongrowing cases; contents are uploaded every run.
Sequential base/current/adapter driver builds took 1.18/3.00/3.01 seconds with existing compiler caches and no competing builds. These are recorded build costs, not comparable cold-compilation measurements. Linux resource timings and cold compilation remain unmeasured. These focused manual cases do not enlarge the normal PR performance matrix.
data.shared-host-execution-comparison#Shared:
The focused selection driver also measures thin and lexical host kernels over seven matching archetypes (512 rows each) alongside six nonmatching archetypes (512 rows each). All matching rows perform the same increment; the closure also counts range invocations. Construction and result checks are excluded, and checks outside the timer verify row count, every row against Bencher.num_iters, and the closure’s exact invocation count and accumulated values. These cases remain manual benchmarks; they are not added to the small PR suite.
On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the shared host setup refactor in 1cd32ba was compared with 688fb670c87ced6b08c920e2c3527a1890218c6f using the same updated driver and compiler environment. Build one optimized binary against an isolated baseline checkout and one against the current source, without -g, sanitizers, or tracing. Warm each once, then alternate baseline/current order across five paired samples with no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs. data:
Entities may be changed by altering the values / attributes of their components, adding new components, or removing existing components.
This chapter uses the World API directly to demonstrate each operation. In application logic, systems are the principal place for these state changes. A system can access an individual entity through its SystemContext, while updates over all entities matching a filter belong in a kernel.
data.accessing-and-changing-individual-compon:
The values of an entity’s component can be accessed and changed via the get method of World.storage.
from larecs import World, Entity, Filter, Components, SystemContext from std.testing import * @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() A reference to a component can be obtained as follows:
# Add an entity with a component var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) # Get a reference to the position; ref pos = world.storage.get[Position](entity) # We can change the reference. pos.x = 5 assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](entity).x, 5) # We can also replace the component completely. world.storage.get[Position](entity) = Position(10, 0) assert_equal(world.storage.get[Position](entity).x, 10) Of course, accessing a component only works if the entity has the component in question. Accessing a component that the entity does not have will result in an error.
# Add an entity without a velocity component entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) with assert_raises(): # This will result in an error _ = world.storage.get[Velocity](entity) We can check if an entity has a component using the has method.
# Check if the entity has a velocity component if world.storage.has[Velocity](entity): print("Entity has a velocity component") else: print("Entity does not have a velocity component")
data.adding-and-removing-components#Adding an:
Components can be added and removed from entities using the add and remove methods.
# Add an entity without components entity = world.storage.add_entity() # Add components to the entity world.storage.add(entity, Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 1)) # Remove a component from the entity world.storage.remove[Velocity](entity) This works with arbitrary numbers of components, so we can add or remove any number of components at once.
If we want to remove some components and replace them with other components directly, we can use the replace method in combination with the by method. The replace method takes Components to be removed as parameters, whereas the by method takes the new components to be added.
# Replace the position component with a velocity component world.storage.replace[Position]().by(Velocity(2, 2), entity=entity) Similar to the add and remove methods, this works with arbitrary numbers of components, so we can replace any number of components with any other number of new components.
Tip
Replacing components in one go is significantly more efficient than removing and adding components separately.
Batch operations Sometimes you need to add or remove components from multiple entities at once. Larecs🌲 provides batch operations that are more efficient than performing individual operations on each entity.
Tip
Batch operations are significantly more efficient than individual operations when working with large numbers of entities, as they minimize memory reorganization and improve cache locality.
Use add, remove, and replace for filtered batch changes. Each returns a locked selection containing only rows actually modified:
var context = SystemContext(world) var created = context.add_entities(Position(0, 0), count=10) created.add[ Velocity, filter=Filter().include[Position].exclude[Velocity]() ](Velocity(1.0, 0.5)) An omitted selection-operation filter means no restriction beyond the saved membership. A supplied filter is intersected with that membership; skipped rows are unchanged and leave the selection’s updated membership. Kernel filter mismatches simply skip rows, but invalid component requests still raise.
created.remove[Velocity]() Selection replacement uses a compile-time Components list for removed types; the replacement value types are inferred from the arguments. This direct form avoids an intermediate builder that would also need to own the lock.
created.replace[ remove=Components[Position](), ](Velocity(2.0, 2.0)) created^.release() Important
Selection component-changing calls mutate the same object and return nothing. Validation errors preserve its membership and lock, so it can be used again. Release it explicitly when finished, or use a with block for cleanup.
data.setting-multiple-components-at-once#Sett:
We can set the values of multiple components at once using the set method. This method takes an arbitrary number of components and sets them all in one go.
# Add an entity with two components entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 1)) # Set multiple components at once world.storage.set(entity, Position(5, 5), Velocity(2, 2))

Use entities for identities and components for per-particle values. Start with the complete movement program.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): """Where a particle is.""" var x: Float64 """Horizontal coordinate.""" var y: Float64 """Vertical coordinate.""" @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): """How far a particle moves per unit of time.""" var dx: Float64 """Horizontal speed.""" var dy: Float64 """Vertical speed.""" var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3))
data.components-and-tags#Components and tags: A component is a Copyable, Movable value; each entity has at most one value of each component type. A tag is a component with no fields: its presence carries the information. Filters can require or exclude it just like a data component.
data.entity-identity#Entity identity: An Entity is a copyable ID and generation, not a component address. Keep the handle to find the particle again through HostStorage.get. Deletion invalidates that identity; recycling an ID increments its generation. Handles belong to their world: do not use a handle in another world.
data.references-after-changes#References afte: Changing Position.x changes a value. Adding or removing a component changes composition and may move rows. Creation, deletion, and other structural changes can invalidate component references and row accessors. Retain entity handles, then reacquire references after mutation. Never use a row index as identity.
data.world-type-packs#World type packs:
World declares all allowed component types at compile time. World[Position, Velocity] allows either, both, or neither on an entity. Resources have separate storage and do not belong in that component pack. Entities with the same component set belong to an archetype; you need no storage layout knowledge to create them or run systems over them.
Use HostStorage.add_entity for initial setup and individual creation. Use systems and kernels for repeated simulation work and scoped structural changes for batches.

data:
Larecs🌲 is an entity component system (ECS) framework for Mojo. The ECS concept is composed of three principal elements:
Entities represent game objects or simulation entities, like individuals in a population model. Components are the data associated to entities, i.e. their properties or state variables. Systems contain the game or simulation logic that reads and mutates ECS state. They use a system context to access the world and to run kernels over filtered sets of components. In an ECS, each entity is “composed of” an arbitrary set of components that can be added and removed at run-time. This modular design enables the development of highly flexible and reusable games or simulations. By decoupling the logic (systems) from the data (entities and components), ECS avoids convoluted inheritance hierarchies and eliminates hard-coded behavior. Instead, entities can be composed of components to exhibit diverse behaviors without sacrificing modularity.
An ECS engine manages this architecture within a central storage structure known as the “World”. The engine handles common tasks such as maintaining entity lists, spawning or deleting entities, and scheduling logic operations, simplifying the development process for users.
Larecs🌲 provides a high-performance ECS framework, empowering developers to create games and simulation models with exceptional flexibility and efficiency.
data.components#Components:
Components are the data associated with entities, characterizing their state and properties. Components are represented via structs: each component type is a different struct. For example, if we want to model a world in which entities may have a position and a velocity, we need to define a Position and a Velocity struct.
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 These structs are not only used to store data. Their types are also used as unique identifiers for the components of an entity. That is, they have a similar role to a key in a dictionary.
How components can be assigned to entities is described in the following chapters.
A component type can be any Copyable & Deinitable struct, including one that owns heap memory, such as a List field. Kernels add requirements for the components they access, depending on where they run:
Execution Requirement for accessed components Sequential host (default) None beyond Copyable & Deinitable Threaded host (experimental) Pointer-free value with trivial copy, move, and destruction Device (experimental) Conforms to TrivialRegisterPassable A kernel that accesses an ineligible component fails to compile. Storage operations and queries accept every component type.
Prefer plain values such as Position and Velocity. When entities change archetype or are removed, Larecs runs the move constructors and destructors of owning components row by row, and such components cannot be used by threaded or device kernels.
data.entities#Entities:
Entities are the central unit around which the data in an ECS is organized. Entities could represent game objects, or potentially anything else that “lives” in a game or simulation. Each entity can possess an arbitrary set of components, which can also be used to characterize an entity. That is, in an ECS, cars would not be directly identified as “cars” but rather as something that has the components Position, Velocity, Fuel reserves, Engine power, etc.
The components are not stored in individual objects but rather in a central container, called the World. Hence, an Entity is merely an identifier that allows retrieving the corresponding components from the world. As such, entities are strictly bound to the world they live in, but also small in memory and easy to store.
Note
Though entities can safely be stored and passed around, their components (or pointers to them) should never be stored externally, as they can move in memory at any time.
How entities are created and used is discussed in the next chapters.
data.the-world#The world:
The central data structure of Larecs🌲 is the World. It stores all data and information about the state of the entities and their surroundings. The World struct provides the main functionality of the ECS, such as adding and removing entities, looking up components, and iterating over entities.
Larecs🌲 gains efficiency and usability by exploiting Mojo’s compile-time programming capabilities. To that end, it needs to know ahead of time which components might turn up in the world, and the World must be statically parameterized with the component types upon creation. This also has the advantage that certain errors can already be prevented at compile time, which makes the program safer and faster.
To set up a World, simply import it from the larecs package and create a World instance as follows:
from larecs import World def main(): # Create a world with the components Position and Velocity var world = World[Position, Velocity]()

data: Iterating over entities can be done via classic for loops applied to queries. Queries provide read-only access to their results. In application logic, systems are the principal place for mutations; use a kernel to update components across all entities matching a filter.
data.iterating-over-queries#Iterating over qu:
As we have seen, we can iterate over queries using a for loop. Here, the control variable (“entity”) is an ArchetypeRowAccessor object, i.e., not technically an Entity, which is merely an identifier of an entity. Instead, the ArchetypeRowAccessor directly provides methods to get and check the existence of components, so that we do not need to call the storage’s methods for this, making the code more efficient. Since query’s iterator gives read-only access, components can only be read this way, not written. Use a kernel from a system to mutate matching components.
Because a query’s filter guarantees which components every matching entity has, get checks its component type against that filter at compile time: requesting a component the filter didn’t include is a compile error, not a runtime one. For a component the filter doesn’t guarantee – typically one you only conditionally access after checking has – use unsafe_get instead, which checks at runtime and raises if the component is missing.
for entity in world.storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()](): ref pos = entity.get[Position]() print( "Entity at position: (" + String(pos.x) + ", " + String(pos.y) + ")" ) if entity.has[Velocity](): # `Velocity` isn't included by this query's filter, so it isn't # guaranteed to exist on every matching entity -- `get` would be # a compile error here. `unsafe_get` is the checked-at-runtime # escape hatch for exactly this case. ref vel = entity.unsafe_get[Velocity]() # Also print the velocity print( " - with velocity (" + String(vel.dx) + ", " + String(vel.dy) + ")" ) Note
The ArchetypeRowAccessor is a temporary object that is created for each iteration. Therefore, it should not be stored in a container. Use ArchetypeRowAccessor.get_entity instead if you need to store the entity for later use.
data.processing-components-with-kernels#Proce:
A kernel is a component-processing function passed to SystemContext.run or EntitySelection.run. It receives a KernelContext and iterates over the entities matching its filter. The filter declares which components the kernel can write and which it can only read. The same kernel can run on the host or, for supported component types, an accelerator device.
The move_entities kernel declared above writes Position and only reads Velocity. The following direct construction demonstrates how the context invokes it:
var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[move_entities]() Calling the same kernel through a selection intersects the kernel filter with the selection’s saved ranges. The selection remains reusable; execution does not change its membership. Host row indices are local to each selected range, while device rows index the packed launch, so neither is a stable entity or selection-wide index.
In an application, the scheduler supplies this context to each system’s lifecycle methods, and the system calls run from there. The system is the scheduled unit of application logic; the kernel is the function it delegates filtered component processing to. See Systems and the scheduler for the complete pattern.
With partitioned spatial storage, ordinary queries traverse all matching blocks and staging rows. Logical archetype composition and query membership stay the same; row indices name a physical store and are not stable identifiers. Query locks and independent copy cursors apply across block boundaries too.
Queries return iteration.LockedEntityRange through HostStorage.Iterator. They share immutable store indices across copies; each copy owns its traversal position and a separate structural lock. Query access stays read-only. For execution on changed rows, use SystemContext batch operations and EntitySelection.run; low-level storage ranges are described in batch creation.
data.queries#Queries:
The query method of HostStorage allows to iterate over all entities with or without a specific set of components. It takes a compile-time Filter specifying the components that each entity we look for must have (and, optionally, must not have). For example, if we want to iterate over all entities with a Position and a Velocity component, we can do this as follows:
from larecs import World, Filter, SystemContext, KernelContext @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position].read[Velocity]() def move_entities(context: KernelContext[move_filter]): for entity in context: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() ref vel = entity.get[Velocity]() pos.x += vel.dx pos.y += vel.dy def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add entities with different components _ = world.storage.add_entity() _ = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0)) _ = world.storage.add_entity(Velocity(1, 0)) _ = world.storage.add_entity(Position(1, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) # Query all entities that have a position. var query = world.storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()]() # Of the entities we have just added, # two have a position component print(len(query)) # "2" # Query iterators are copyable. A copy starts at the same position. var query_copy = query.copy() # Now let us iterate over the queried entities # (`^` transfers this iterator into the loop without copying it). for entity in query^: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() print( "Entity at position: (" + String(pos.x) + ", " + String(pos.y) + ")" ) # The copy has an independent cursor, so it can be consumed separately. for _ in query_copy^: pass The filter can also exclude entities that have certain components. For example, if we want to iterate over all entities that have a Position component but not a Velocity component, we can do this using exclude:
var excluding_query = world.storage.query[ Filter().include[Position].exclude[Velocity]() ]() print(len(excluding_query)) # "1" Furthermore, we can also query for entities that have exactly the components we are looking for but no more. This can be done using exclusive. For example, if we want to iterate over all entities that have only a Position component, we can do this as follows:
var exclusive_query = world.storage.query[ Filter().include[Position].exclusive() ]() print(len(exclusive_query)) # "1" Note
Determining the length of a query is not a trivial operation and may require an internal iteration if the ECS involves many components. Therefore, it is advisable to avoid applying the len function to queries in “hot” code. Nonetheless, the len function is much faster than counting entities manually by iterating over a query.

data:
Not all data in a world is associated with
specific entities. This often applies to
parameters (such as a time step),
global state variables (such as the current time),
or spatial data structures (such as a grid displaying
entity positions). These data are called resources.
data.adding-and-accessing-resources#Adding an:
The examples below access a World directly to introduce the resource API. During application execution, resource changes should generally be owned by a system, keeping them in the same scheduled lifecycle as entity and component changes. Its lifecycle methods can access resources through context.world[].resources.
Resources can be accessed and added via the resources field of World. Adding a resource is done via the resources.add method:
def main() raises: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() # Add the `Time` resource world.resources.add(Time(0.0)) The resources attribute also allows us to access and change resources via get and set. Unlike their component-related counterparts, these operations need no entity argument: a resource is selected only by its type.
ResourceStorage.get intentionally returns a reference with UnsafeAnyOrigin, preserving the mutability of the storage access. It should keep this origin until Mojo’s origin system can model the ownership relation between the resource container and its separately allocated resource values. Tying the returned reference to the storage origin is not a suitable interim replacement.
# Change a resource value via a reference world.resources.get[Time]().delta = 1.0 # Get a reference to a resource ref time = world.resources.get[Time]() # Change the resource value via the reference time.delta = 2.0 # Replace the entire resource through the returned reference world.resources.get[Time]() = Time(3.0) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Time]().delta, 3.0) The add and set methods can add or set multiple resources at once. For example, consider the additional resources Temperature and SelectedEntities, each defined just like Time above.
We can add and set them as follows:
# Add multiple resources world.resources.add( Temperature(20.0), SelectedEntities(List[Entity]()) ) # Set multiple resources world.resources.set( Temperature(30.0), Time(2.0) ) These operations are strict by default:
add raises if a requested resource type already exists. get and remove raise if the requested resource does not exist. set raises if any requested resource does not exist and does not update any of them. Use set[add_if_not_found=True](...) when missing resources should be inserted. For example, set can explicitly recreate a missing resource:
world.resources.remove[Temperature]() world.resources.set[add_if_not_found=True](Temperature(25.0)) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Temperature]().temperature, 25.0) Like components, resources can own heap memory, as SelectedEntities does with its List. A world holds at most one value per resource type, so a resource suits data of any size that the whole simulation shares. Owning resources work in sequential host kernels; threaded and device kernels need a pointer-free value or an adapter, as described in Using resources in kernels.
# Create entities and add them to the selected entities for i in range(10): var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(Float64(i), Float64(i))) world.resources.get[SelectedEntities]().entities.append(entity)
data.defining-resources#Defining resources:
Similar to components, resources are defined via structs. That is, each resource has a specific type, and having two resources of the same type is not possible.
However, in contrast to components, the (potentially) used resources do not need to be known at compile time but can be dynamically added to the world and are keyed by their runtime type name.
from larecs import ( ExecutionBackend, World, Entity, SystemContext, KernelContext, Filter, Resources, ResourceType, ) from std.testing import assert_equal, assert_false, assert_true @fieldwise_init struct Time(ResourceType, TrivialRegisterPassable): var delta: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Temperature(ResourceType): var temperature: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct SelectedEntities(ResourceType): var entities: List[Entity] @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): var x: Float64 var y: Float64 @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): var dx: Float64 var dy: Float64 A resource must conform to ResourceType (Copyable & Deinitable). SelectedEntities owns a List, which sequential host kernels accept. Device and threaded kernels check a resource’s representation rather than a declared trait: Time and Temperature both qualify because they hold only a Float64. Time additionally declares TrivialRegisterPassable, which these checks do not require.
data.invocation-lifetime-and-failures#Invocat:
run completes synchronously. Larecs retains sources and descriptors throughout execution, rejects reentrant lookup/replacement/removal of bound sources, and rejects duplicate source declarations. Previously escaped UnsafeAnyOrigin references must not mutate or resize the source while a kernel uses its view; views and references must not escape the invocation. Copying or destroying leased storage through an escaped alias aborts because lifecycle operations cannot raise.
Device component, capture, and resource downloads use owned staging and publish only after synchronization succeeds. On failure Larecs drains the queue and propagates the error; if completion remains unknown, further execution on the world raises. Failed calls discard staged outputs, without promising rollback of other host effects. Empty device matches still validate resources and adapters but perform no device allocation, upload, or launch.
data.mutable-adapted-resources-experimental#M:
An adapter can also give kernels a writer view, so shared output such as a per-cell grid is filled without a MutCapture and with the same kernel on every target. The access declaration selects the view:
Declaration get[T]() returns Output before the kernel runs Resources().read[T]() T.View[False] Not applicable Resources().write[T]() T.View[True] Fresh, initialized by the adapter Resources().read_write[T]() T.View[True] Existing contents preserved Read and writer views can be different types:
struct GridAdapter(ResourceAdapter): comptime Source = Grid comptime View[mutable: Bool] = GridFill if mutable else GridRead comptime supports_mutation = True comptime supports_concurrent_mutation = True Both capabilities default to False. supports_mutation admits write and read_write declarations for sequential host runs. Device and threaded=True runs also require supports_concurrent_mutation. Declare it only if every writer-view operation is safe under concurrent use, for example because slots are reserved with atomics and then written disjointly. Larecs leases the source exclusively for the invocation. This does not prevent races between the GPU threads or host workers of one kernel: you are responsible for safe resource access. Unsupported combinations fail compilation.
The descriptor a kernel receives is immutable. A writer view holds pointers to adapter-managed backing buffers, such as slots, per-cell counters, reductions, and error flags, and mutates them through its own methods. Mutable adapters implement four hooks that receive the full ResourceAccess mode, so write can initialize fresh output while read_write preserves it:
Hook When Larecs calls it bind_host_mutable[access](mut source) Once before host kernels run. On the host, kernels write the source’s buffers directly. Also called for device runs without matching rows. prepare_device_mutable[access](mut source, mut cache) Once before a device launch. Use cache.fill for fresh output and cache.upload_mutable to preserve contents. stage_device_results[access](mut source, mut cache) After the launch is queued. Stage every output with cache.download. finalize[access](mut source) Once after all kernel work completed and device outputs were published. Use it to clamp counters or report overflow. Preparation and finalization run once per invocation, across every matching archetype, selected range, threaded chunk, and device launch, including runs with no matching rows. Output is never reset per archetype or worker. Device runs use the world’s device queue and cache; buffers and staging stay alive until completion. Mutable adapted sources are prepared on every run, even in worlds that reuse device copies. Size host targets before staging downloads; they are written only after the queue completes.
Failures follow the invocation rules:
Host writes are not rolled back. If preparation fails after write initialization, the source stays initialized, and finalize does not run. Device outputs are published only after synchronization succeeds. A failed run discards them. If finalize raises, the run raises, but published outputs remain and the world stays usable. examples/scatter_resource.mojo is a complete example. Writers reserve per-cell slots with atomic counters and count dropped writes; finalize clamps the counters. The same thin kernel runs sequentially, threaded, and on a device. Run it with pixi run scatter-example. Slot order within a cell depends on scheduling.
Migrating existing adapters Adapters written for the read-only API need three changes:
Replace comptime View = MyView with comptime View[mut: Bool] = MyView. Change bind_host and prepare_device to return Self.View[False]. Remove comptime KernelView = MyView from the source. KernelView still exists as an alias for View[False]. Adapters that do not opt into mutation keep their behavior. Mutable declarations of them now fail with “mutable access requires Adapter.supports_mutation”.
data.portable-owning-resources#Portable ownin:
Use BufferResource for a contiguous scalar collection. The same kernel requests the original source type and receives its read-only ReadBuffer view on both backends:
from larecs import ExecutionBackend, BufferResource, Filter, KernelContext, Resources, SystemContext, World comptime Samples = BufferResource[DType.int32] comptime required = Resources().read[Samples]() def add_sample(context: KernelContext[Filter().include[Int32](), required]): ref samples = context.resources.get[Samples]() for entity in context: entity.get[Int32]() += samples[0] def main() raises: var world = World[Int32]() world.resources.add(Samples([Int32(7), Int32(8)])) _ = world.storage.add_entities(Int32(1), count=37) var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[add_sample]() context.run[add_sample, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() world.resources.get[Samples]().samples[0] = 9 context.run[add_sample]() Device execution requires a working accelerator. By default, the samples are uploaded on every device run; worlds that reuse unchanged device copies skip the upload while the source is unchanged. Device allocation capacity is reused. The host source remains unchanged by device view access. ReadBuffer has len and bounds-checked indexing; empty buffers have length zero and must not be indexed.
Defining a custom portable resource Implement DevicePassableResource when your resource owns data that cannot be copied directly to a device, or needs a domain-specific kernel API. Keep the owning host type, its kernel view, and transfer logic separate:
Type Contains Used by Grid Owning List and current dimensions Application code between runs GridView Immutable sample pointer, dimensions, and sampling methods The same kernel on either backend GridAdapter Static validation and view preparation methods Larecs during run The source declares its Adapter as a compile-time member. The adapter declares the matching Source and a View[mut: Bool] mapping; it needs no constructor or instance fields. A read-only adapter maps both access kinds to one view type. The source’s View and KernelView (an alias for View[False]) default to the adapter’s mapping. Every method reads the current source, including configuration such as dimensions.
This complete example uses a rectangular grid. Its view exposes last() to keep pointer arithmetic inside the resource API. A scientific view can instead provide interpolation, coordinate lookup, or other read-only operations.
# SKIP_DEBUG # SKIP_ASAN from std.sys import has_accelerator from std.testing import assert_equal from larecs import ( ExecutionBackend, DevicePassableResource, ResourceAdapter, ResourceDeviceCache, Filter, KernelContext, Resources, SystemContext, World, ) @fieldwise_init struct Grid(DevicePassableResource): """Owns current host samples and grid metadata.""" comptime Adapter = GridAdapter var values: List[Int32] var width: Int var height: Int @fieldwise_init struct GridView(TrivialRegisterPassable): """Portable read-only descriptor over current target-local samples.""" var values: Pointer[Int32, ImmUntrackedOrigin] var width: Int var height: Int def last(self) -> Int32: """Reads the last sample of this validated nonempty grid. Returns: Last grid sample. """ return self.values[unsafe_offset=self.width * self.height - 1] struct GridAdapter(ResourceAdapter): """Stateless adapter using current dimensions and cached sample capacity.""" comptime Source = Grid comptime View[mut: Bool] = GridView @staticmethod def validate(source: Self.Source) raises: """Checks a nonempty rectangular grid before preparing either target. Args: source: Current host owner. Raises: Error: If dimensions overflow or do not match sample storage. """ if source.width <= 0 or source.height <= 0: raise Error("This grid requires positive dimensions") if source.width > 9223372036854775807 // source.height: raise Error("Grid dimensions overflow") if source.width * source.height != len(source.values): raise Error("Grid dimensions must match sample count") @staticmethod def bind_host(source: Self.Source) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Borrows immutable samples from the validated host owner. Args: source: Current validated source. Raises: Error: If descriptor preparation fails. Returns: Descriptor over host samples. """ return { Pointer[Int32, ImmUntrackedOrigin]( unsafe_from_address=Int(source.values.unsafe_ptr()) ), source.width, source.height, } @staticmethod def prepare_device( source: Self.Source, mut cache: ResourceDeviceCache ) raises -> Self.View[False]: """Uploads current samples and returns the same descriptor type. Args: source: Current validated source. cache: Source-type, context-local allocation cache. Raises: Error: If sample allocation or upload fails. Returns: Descriptor over device samples. """ return { cache.upload[Int32](0, Span(source.values)), source.width, source.height, } validate runs before preparation on either backend, even when no entities match. Check sample counts and arithmetic here; a trivial view descriptor does not prove that its pointer indexing is valid. This grid rejects empty storage, so last() is always defined after successful validation.
bind_host borrows the owner’s samples without copying. Its untracked immutable pointer relies on Larecs retaining the source throughout the invocation; it must never point into a temporary local collection. prepare_device uploads the samples through the supplied cache and returns the same descriptor with a device pointer. Larecs uploads the descriptor itself; the adapter does not need to.
Registering and using the custom resource Declare read access using the source type, and keep that same type in get[Grid](). Inside the kernel the result is an immutable GridView, on both host and device. Outside the kernel, world.resources.get[Grid]() returns the owning Grid for edits. The following continues the example above:
comptime required = Resources().read[Grid]() def add_grid_sample( context: KernelContext[Filter().include[Int32](), required] ): """Adds the grid's last sample to each matching component. Args: context: Component rows and the read-only GridView binding. """ ref grid = context.resources.get[Grid]() for entity in context: entity.get[Int32]() += grid.last() def main() raises: """Uses one custom resource and kernel on the host and, if available, device. Raises: Error: If resource validation, execution, or a result check fails. """ var world = World[Int32]() world.resources.add(Grid([Int32(1), Int32(2), Int32(3), Int32(9)], 2, 2)) var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Int32(1)) var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[add_grid_sample]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 10) # World-side access returns the owning Grid, so samples can be edited. world.resources.get[Grid]().values[3] = 5 context.run[add_grid_sample]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 15) comptime if has_accelerator(): context.run[add_grid_sample, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() assert_equal(world.storage.get[Int32](entity), 20) assert_equal(world.resources.get[Grid]().values[3], 5) The host calls always run; the device call runs when an accelerator is available. No explicit binding registration or manual transfer is required. Editing the owner between runs changes what the next invocation sees. Kernel results go to components; the read-only resource is never downloaded or changed by the kernel. Host-only resources can continue implementing ResourceType without an adapter.
Adapter allocation and access rules Every adapter must support concurrent reads of its read view, View[False], on the view’s execution target. View methods and all reachable memory must permit concurrent reads without hidden unsafe mutation. No escaped alias may mutate, resize, relocate, or free backing data before invocation completion; immutable pointer fields alone do not establish this guarantee. This is a universal adapter contract, with no capability marker.
Threaded host calls accept adapted sources only through explicit read declarations. The caller validates and binds each source once, then shares the same descriptor and sample storage across jobs. Resource leases and descriptor owners remain alive until all workers join, including whole-range fallback. Ordinary pointer-free read resources also work without an adapter. Ordinary mutable resources remain unsupported by this engine; mutable adapted resources require concurrent mutation support.
Use nonnegative cache slots for sample allocations. Slot -1 is reserved for Larecs’s view descriptor. For multiple arrays, give each array its own stable slot, such as 0 for samples and 1 for coordinates. Each world keeps a separate cache per source type, tied to its device context. Capacity is reused, and every preparation uploads current contents. Adapters need no revision tracking of their own: in worlds that reuse device copies, Larecs skips prepare_device entirely while the source is unchanged.
The cache accepts supported pointer-free trivial sample values, snapshots them in native owned staging, and returns an immutable device pointer. Adapters must use cache-owned allocations and this upload helper; queued copies from external host pointers or pointers to temporary allocations violate the lifetime contract. Views may contain immutable pointers and trivial metadata; mutable pointer fields are rejected. Adapters remain responsible for valid device addresses and pointee interpretation.
There is no adapter factory or instance. Registration happens automatically on add and insert-on-set; source types identify bindings, so two resources may share the same view type. A wrapper can adapt a third-party owner. See the compiled grid example.
Adapters without mutation support accept only read, including on the host; Resources[AdaptedSource]() and mutable declarations fail compilation. get[Source]() always returns the associated view; kernels cannot access the owner. Edit the world-side owner between runs, including whole-instance assignment through world.resources.get[T]() = T(...); the next run validates and uploads the new source without rebinding. Copied worlds have independent host owners and empty resource caches.
data.removing-resources#Removing resources:
One or multiple resources can be removed via the remove method. The existence of a resource is checked via the has method.
When removing multiple types, removals happen in argument order. If a later type is missing, remove raises after any earlier types have already been removed. Check all types with has first when the operation must be all-or-nothing.
# Remove the `Time` and the `Temperature` resource world.resources.remove[Time, Temperature]() # Check if the `Time` resource exists assert_false(world.resources.has[Time]()) # `set[add_if_not_found=True]` can insert it again world.resources.set[add_if_not_found=True](Time(4.0)) assert_true(world.resources.has[Time]())
data.resource-permissions#Resource permission:
Resources[T]() preserves read_write access. Prefer explicit declarations:
comptime required = Resources().read[Time]().read_write[Statistics]() A read getter is immutable and its device buffer is never downloaded. read_write permits mutable get[T]() and copies device changes back after successful completion. Host write[T]() offers set[T](value) only; it rejects get[T](). Device write-only resources are unsupported because conditional shared writes could publish uninitialized data. Applications must synchronize concurrent writes to ordinary shared resources themselves.
data.reusing-unchanged-device-copies-experime:
By default every backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE run uploads all resources and readable component columns it declares, even if they did not change. Worlds that call world.reuse_device_copies(True) skip uploads of data that is unchanged since its device copy was made. For adapted resources this skips the whole prepare_device call; validation and leases still run on every call. Written data is still downloaded after every run.
Larecs cannot see what you do with a reference after it returns it. It tracks revisions that advance on every Larecs access that may mutate data:
Resources: add, set, get through a mutable world, host runs declaring write or read_write, and device runs writing the resource. Component columns, per type and physical store: world.storage.get and set, kernel runs writing the type, and every structural change, spatial reordering, or partition move of the store. Use world.resources.read[T]() and world.storage.read[T](entity) for reads between device runs: they return immutable references and keep device copies reusable, whereas get on a mutable world always counts as a mutation. Read queries never count as mutations.
Component columns are reused per contiguous store range. Kernels with different filters on the same component type pack stores at different offsets, so alternating them uploads that column again each time.
Re-obtain or invalidate. In a world that reuses device copies, never mutate a resource through a reference obtained before a later Larecs call or through a raw pointer without telling Larecs. Re-obtain the reference with get after each run, or call world.resources.invalidate_device[T]() (or world.invalidate_device_copies() for everything) after the mutation. Otherwise the next device run silently reads the stale device copy.
world.reuse_device_copies(True) # Reading through `read` keeps an unchanged device copy reusable. _ = world.resources.read[Time]().delta # A pointer kept across runs bypasses revision tracking... var time_ptr = Pointer(to=world.resources.get[Time]()) time_ptr[].delta = 4.0 # ...so invalidate after mutating through it. world.resources.invalidate_device[Time]() world.reuse_device_copies(False) A failed device run marks the copies it touched as unknown, so the next run uploads them again. Disabling reuse, removing a resource, and copying the world discard device copy records.
data.using-resources-in-kernels#Using resourc:
A kernel declares the resource types it may access with a compile-time Resources list. Pass that list as the second parameter of KernelContext, then retrieve a resource through context.resources.get[T]():
var mover = world.storage.add_entity( Position(0.0, 0.0), Velocity(2.0, 1.0) ) def move_with_time( context: KernelContext[ Filter().include[Position].read[Velocity](), Resources[Time](), ] ): ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for entity in context: ref pos = entity.get[Position]() ref vel = entity.get[Velocity]() pos.x += vel.dx * time.delta pos.y += vel.dy * time.delta var context = SystemContext(world) context.run[move_with_time]() # `Time.delta` is 2.0, so the velocity moved the entity by (4.0, 2.0) ref position = world.storage.get[Position](mover) assert_equal(position.x, 4.0) assert_equal(position.y, 2.0) Here, Resources[Time]() makes Time available to move_with_time. get[Time]() returns a mutable reference, so a kernel may also update the resource. Such changes remain in the world’s resource storage after the kernel finishes. Every declared resource must already have been added to the world; otherwise SystemContext.run raises an error.
The direct SystemContext construction keeps this example focused on the resource API. In application logic, call run from a system lifecycle method, as shown in Systems and the scheduler.
A resource is one shared mutable value for every entity processed by the kernel. Concurrent reads need no special handling. Writes from GPU threads must be synchronized or otherwise made race-free; in particular, do not update a shared resource once per entity without an atomic or reduction strategy. Writing per-entity results to components and reducing them in a separate step is often simpler. Keep side effects inside the entity loop, because the number of kernel calls depends on the execution target:
Sequential host: one call per non-empty matching physical store. With spatial partitioning, one archetype can have several physical stores. EntitySelection.run calls the kernel once per selected row range instead. Threaded host: one call per kernel chunk; each store or selected range is split into chunks that may run concurrently. Device: one launch covers all matching rows. Host kernels may also capture surrounding values and access resources through context.run(kernel). See Capturing host kernels for an example. Device entry points use the non-capturing context.run[kernel]() form.
Import ExecutionBackend from larecs and replace the host run call with:
context.run[move_with_time, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() Host execution is the default. DEVICE requires a working accelerator and raises when unavailable, including for empty matches; it never falls back to HOST.
For device execution, components must conform to TrivialRegisterPassable. Ordinary resources need a supported pointer-free representation with trivial copy, move, and destruction. Numeric values, Bool, and aggregates of those values are accepted without declaring TrivialRegisterPassable. Owning collections, host pointers, and opaque representations (including fixed Array fields in this increment) are rejected. Host kernels still support owning resources.
